solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, enumeration length); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing; the grid proves the blog's answer wrong at 6 down, corrected here

entries.clue: Irritation seeing ID number not fully entered (7)

indicatorNotes.not fully: A word given not fully is given short of its whole, so its last letter goes.

blocks.note: a PIN is a personal identification number
KEYED = entered (data), cut short by one letter

annotation.surface: Someone is annoyed at having only half typed in their ID number.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Entered' looks like a container instruction but is a plain synonym: keyed in, as at a keypad.
annotation.definitionFit: The everyday name for conjunctivitis, an eye complaint whose main symptom is a red, itchy irritation.

entries.clue: Notices point up uses for rest areas (3,5)

indicatorNotes.up: In a down clue the letters are written top to bottom, so sending them up reads them backwards.

annotation.surface: A notice board announces what the lay-bys are for.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words go up together: SPOTS then TIP, read from the bottom, gives PIT STOPS.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose sense: places where travellers pull off the road for a break, as racing cars pull into the pits.

entries.clue: Charlie’s insensitive finishing short row on the phone (8)

indicatorNotes.finishing short: A word that finishes short stops before its end, so its last letter is lost.
indicatorNotes.on the phone: Over the phone you only hear a word, so what counts is its sound, not its spelling.

blocks.note: NUMB = insensitive, losing its last letter

annotation.surface: Charlie is being unfeeling, cutting short a phone argument.
annotation.walkthrough: A charlie is British slang for a fool. 'Row' looks like a quarrel, which suits the phone, but it is rowing a boat.
annotation.definitionFit: A British slang synonym: a charlie is a silly, foolish person, as is a thickhead.

entries.clue: Eastern state limiting society’s composition (5)

indicatorNotes.limiting: To limit something is to set bounds around it, so SAY closes round the S.

blocks.note: S = society, placed just after SAY's first letter

annotation.surface: An eastern state keeps a tight rein on how its society is made up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'State' reads as a country, but it is the verb. S(S)AY after E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from school: a composition is a short piece of written prose.

entries.clue: After hours learning, becoming smoother around girls (7,7)

annotation.surface: Someone learns charm late at night, getting slicker with women.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Around' is not a container here; it is the abbreviation C, as in 'c. 1850'.
annotation.definitionFit: Courses held once the working day is over, so learning done after hours.

entries.clue: Second best comedian (6)

blocks.note: the cream is the best of anything

annotation.surface: A ranking of comics: this one came runner-up.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a runner-up, but 'second' only gives S.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: a very funny person is called a scream, which a good comedian is.

entries.clue: Smoke fish in Calais and specify boxes (9)

indicatorNotes.boxes: To box something is to shut it inside a container, so CITE closes round the rest.

blocks.note: a gar is a long-snouted fish

annotation.surface: Instructions for smoking fish in a French port and stating how it is packed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Smoke' looks like a verb for curing fish; it is the noun. CI(GAR ET)TE.
annotation.definitionFit: Informally 'a smoke' is anything smoked, and the commonest such thing is a rolled tube of tobacco.

entries.clue: Imagine not keeping the first cryptic puzzle (6)

indicatorNotes.not keeping the first: The word does not keep its first letter, so that letter is dropped.
indicatorNotes.cryptic: Cryptic means hidden or obscured, so the letters are disguised by jumbling.

annotation.surface: Try to picture a crossword without its opening clue.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cryptic puzzle' looks like one phrase, the definition; 'cryptic' is the anagram indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something baffling or mysterious that needs working out.

entries.clue: Simple ways to save oxygen (6)

indicatorNotes.save: Save can mean except ('all save one'), so TO is taken except its O.

blocks.note: TO without the letter for oxygen

annotation.surface: Advice on easy ways of conserving oxygen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Save' looks like conserving; here it means except.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of unpretentious, as a modest meal or house is a simple one.

entries.clue: Final irony, a musician batting at No 11 (5,2,3,4)

blocks.note: No 11 is last in the batting order, the tail

annotation.surface: A rock star going in last for a cricket team is quite a twist.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket the weak batters at the bottom of the order are called the tail, and No 11 is the very last of them.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for a nasty twist kept for the end, as a scorpion keeps its sting.

entries.clue: Inflated spare tyre going down, losing diameter (9)

indicatorNotes.losing: A word losing something has it taken away, here the D.

blocks.note: a spare tyre is a paunch, a tum (stomach)

annotation.surface: A pumped-up spare wheel deflates as its diameter shrinks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spare tyre' is the roll of fat round a waist, not a wheel; tum is British for stomach.
annotation.definitionFit: A formal synonym: swollen or puffed up, as an inflated thing is.

entries.clue: In mid-August one replaces a dull routine (5)

indicatorNotes.replaces: One thing replacing another takes its place, so I goes where A was.
indicatorNotes.In mid-: The swap is made in the middle of the word, where its A sits.

blocks.note: I = one, the letter moving in

annotation.surface: A late-summer holiday gets swapped for the daily slog.
annotation.walkthrough: August is the adjective (majestic), not the month; its capital is only there because of the hyphen. GR(A→I)ND.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal noun: the daily grind is hard, monotonous work.

entries.clue: Wine beginning to taste tolerable (5)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: The beginning of a word is its first letter.

annotation.surface: A wine that is starting to taste all right.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a wine opening up in the glass; 'beginning to' takes just one letter of 'taste'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a sweet Hungarian dessert wine.

entries.clue: One’s not bright, amusing or original (9)

indicatorNotes.original: Something original is new, so the letters take a new arrangement.

annotation.surface: A put-down: this person is neither clever nor funny nor creative.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Original' reads as a third quality in the list, but it is the anagram indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: Read as 'one who is not bright': an ignorant, dim person.

entries.clue: Girl working with Steptoe and Son, furniture movers (12)

indicatorNotes.working: Letters that are working are in motion, so they move into a new order.

blocks.note: surface padding joining the name to its partner

annotation.surface: A young woman joins Steptoe and Son, the rag-and-bone men, hauling furniture.
annotation.walkthrough: Steptoe and Son was a British sitcom about a father and son in the junk trade, so furniture movers fits the surface. Here it is ghosts that throw furniture about.
annotation.definitionFit: A witty description: these noisy spirits are said to send chairs and tables flying.

entries.clue: Roughly, a can held about one dish (9)

indicatorNotes.Roughly: Roughly means not precisely, so the letters come out in an imprecise order.
indicatorNotes.about: About means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the I.

blocks.note: I = one, the letter held inside

annotation.surface: A rough description of a tin wrapped around a single portion.
annotation.walkthrough: The commas and 'held' suggest a can doing the holding; in fact the jumbled can letters do the holding, round I.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a Mexican dish of rolled, filled tortilla.

entries.clue: Like part of Birmingham? Wow! (8)

blocks.note: Aston is a district of Birmingham

annotation.surface: Someone is amazed by a Birmingham neighbourhood.
annotation.walkthrough: Aston is an inner-city area of Birmingham, England's second city; '-ish' turns it into 'Aston-like'.
annotation.definitionFit: The verb sense of wow: to amaze or impress someone.

entries.clue: Who advance unlawfully seizing power? (8)

indicatorNotes.seizing: To seize is to grab and hold, so the lenders hold the P.

blocks.note: usurers lend (advance) money at illegal rates

annotation.surface: A question about people who push forward illegally to grab control.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: read as wordplay, 'advance' is lending money; read straight, it is people pushing forward to take a throne. USUR(P)ERS.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes those who take a throne or office illegally by force.

entries.clue: Highlights, including 100 Universal recording artists (12)

indicatorNotes.including: A word including others takes them in, so STRESSES holds the rest.

blocks.note: U = universal, a British film rating
an LP is a long-playing record

annotation.surface: A music label's highlights reel of a hundred of its recording stars.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Recording artists' pretends to be one phrase; 'recording' is LP and 'artists' alone is the definition. S(C U LP)TRESSES.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: women who make art in stone or bronze.

entries.clue: What candid people call themselves (6)

blocks.note: the surface wants a self-description, like 'honest'; the setter means the idiom 'call a spade a spade'
the surface points back at the people; the setter means the thing being named, called by its own name

annotation.surface: A question about how frank people describe themselves.
annotation.walkthrough: Frank people are said to 'call a spade a spade', so what they call spades is spades themselves; 'themselves' refers to the tools, not the people.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: plain speakers name digging tools by their plain name, and nothing fancier.

entries.clue: Jack aboard vessel to serve wine (6)

blocks.note: a jack is a ship's flag, as in Union Jack

annotation.surface: A sailor on a ship is serving the wine.
annotation.walkthrough: Jack reads as a sailor, which fits the vessel, but it is the flag flown at a ship's bow.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: a large jug with a handle and spout used for pouring wine.

entries.clue: Sounding friendly, donkey in straw bedding (9)

indicatorNotes.Sounding: Sounding like something means heard as it, so the words are said aloud.

blocks.note: pally = friendly, an ass is a donkey

annotation.surface: A friendly-sounding donkey bedded down in straw.
annotation.walkthrough: Pally is British slang for friendly.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: a thin mattress stuffed with straw.

entries.clue: Speech of many pages some heard in church (5)

indicatorNotes.Speech of: The speech of a word is how it is spoken, so only its sound counts.

blocks.note: a quire is a bundle of about 24 sheets of paper

annotation.surface: A long sermon is partly heard by the congregation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Speech of many pages' looks like a long address; 'speech of' is the sound indicator, and a quire is a paper measure.
annotation.definitionFit: A witty description: a group of singers, some of the people you hear at a church service.

entries.clue: Accessory for the queen or the king to possess (5)

annotation.surface: An item that either the queen or the king might have.
annotation.walkthrough: CR is the royal cipher of King Charles (Latin Carolus Rex).
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: the jewelled headpiece a queen wears on state occasions.

entries.clue: Act leads to more governors overturning a conviction (5)

indicatorNotes.leads to: The leads of words are their leading, first letters.
indicatorNotes.overturning: Overturning something turns it upside down, so the letters come back in reverse.

blocks.note: first letters of more and governors

annotation.surface: A law passes, letting more state governors quash a conviction.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Conviction' reads as a court verdict; it is a firm belief.
annotation.definitionFit: The belief sense of conviction: a firmly held principle not open to question.

entries.clue: Flag rolling ceremony joined by old salt, perhaps (9)

indicatorNotes.rolling: Something rolling turns over, so the word comes back reading backwards.

blocks.note: to flag is to pave with flagstones

annotation.surface: A flag-raising ceremony attended by a veteran sailor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old salt' is a veteran sailor, but 'old' is O and 'salt' belongs to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: rock salt is a mineral deposit left behind when seawater evaporates.

entries.clue: Nudes modelled eating a dessert (6)

indicatorNotes.modelled: Clay that is modelled is shaped into a new form, and so are these letters.
indicatorNotes.eating: Something eating takes food inside, so the jumbled letters take in the A.

blocks.note: as written, the letter taken in

annotation.surface: Life models are having a dessert.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Modelled' fits the art-class nudes, but it is the anagram indicator. SUND(A)E.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: ice cream topped with syrup, nuts or fruit.

entries.clue: Meals left for bishop in batches (7)

indicatorNotes.for: One thing for another means in exchange for it, so L takes B's place.

blocks.note: L = left, the letter moving in
B = bishop in chess notation, the letter moving out

annotation.surface: Meals are dished out in batches, one serving set aside for the bishop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left for bishop' looks like food saved for a cleric; it means L swapped in for B.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the midday meal, one of the day's meals.
